reason: shipment = freight (goods carried); inventory/receipt/premium do not compete.

Link (a): 'pouch' is a narrower word for 'bag'. Dictionaries define a pouch as 'a small bag', so d is a kind of c, which is the 'A kind of' link, not 'Same meaning'. The shown gloss ('a sack or satchel of moderate size') also does not describe a pouch.
handcuff = manacle (one WordNet synset); deterrent/impediment/pillory do not compete; fine at L7.

Link (a): a swamp is one TYPE of wetland (wetlands include marshes, bogs, fens and swamps; WordNet puts swamp under wetland). d is a narrower word, so 'Same meaning' is false and the pair teaches the 'A kind of' link under the wrong name.
accumulation = buildup; melanin/breakdown do not compete.

Link (a): acting is one kind of performing. Singing, dancing, playing music and doing magic are all performing but not acting, so d is narrower than c. A careful child can see 'you can perform a song without acting', so 'Same meaning' is not exactly true.
possible = feasible; probable is a fair near-miss rather than a second answer.
A perfumer makes perfume (MW also gives 'one that perfumes'). It is the only person on offer.
Exact noun form; stimuli/stimulus/activation share no root.
miserable is a stronger sad; ecstatic/patriotic/nostalgic are not.
A gale is a stronger breeze; the false-number gloss is hidden.
hot is a stronger warm; cold/gulp/downpour are not.
A zither is a kind of instrument; fret is a part, saxophone a sibling, and instrumental an adjective.
Exact family pair, and the praise-sense gloss is hidden.
envious = jealous in ordinary use; no option competes.
oval = ellipse (one WordNet synset); round/lob do not compete. Note: the shown gloss stops mid-sentence ('cutting completely…'). Shorten it or hide it.
loud is the opposite of quiet; silent/calm are synonyms and humble is unrelated.
entrance is the opposite of exit; no option competes.
gelatin -> gelatinous is exact; no option shares the root.
continuance is a real noun of continue; no option shares the root.
A synthesizer is a musical instrument; no option is its category.
Marinara is a sauce; no option is its category.

Link (a) and level (d): in everyday and British use, 'extremities' means the hands and feet (Oxford, Cambridge), which are only the ends of the limbs. The 'limb' sense is medical register ('upper/lower extremities'). To an 11-year-old, extremity means 'the farthest point' or 'an extreme'. So only a technical sense matches, and even that is narrower in common use. Too weak and too adult for L4.
The award sense of citation (Cambridge's first sense: a formal statement praising bravery) matches commendation, and the gloss teaches it. condemnation is an opposite and the rest are unrelated.
loyalty = devotion; no option competes.
A bump (on the head) is a swelling; shin/sag/eyelash do not compete.

Level (d) and loose fit: 'elicit' (and 'evoke') are secondary-school academic words, too advanced for L4 (about age 11). They also overlap only in the 'call forth a response' sense: you evoke a memory or an image, but you elicit an answer or information ('the smell elicited memories' is odd). Move it to L7 or above, or cut it.

Link (a): a platter is a large serving plate or dish, while a tray is a flat board with a rim for carrying things (Cambridge). They are related tableware, not the same thing. A cafeteria tray is not a platter, and the gloss shown is tray's 'receptacle' sense, not a dish.
contempt = disdain; insult/affront are acts, not the feeling, and acceptance is unrelated.
legacy = inheritance; the options are people.
A racehorse is a kind of horse; rodeo/equestrian/handler are not its category.
Nutmeg is a spice; the options are other foods, not categories.
beg = entreat; entreat is formal, not archaic, at L5; bully/grumble/shun do not compete.
pig = hog (one WordNet synset), used in the farm-animal sense; hen/pigeon do not compete.
exhaustion = fatigue; no option competes.
crease = wrinkle; no option competes.
customize = personalize; no option competes.

Link (a) and (d): aqua and cyan are two different colour names, not one word's synonyms. Aqua is a light blue-green, and WordNet files it with turquoise/aquamarine. Cyan is a separate synset, 'a primary subtractive color for light', and that technical printer-ink gloss is what the child is shown. Aqua's other sense (water) also pulls the other way. A careful child cannot be sure these 'mean the same'.

Link (a): gruel is defined as 'a THIN porridge' (WordNet puts it under porridge; Oxford: thin liquid food of oatmeal), so porridge is the broader word and gruel a kind of it. That is the 'A kind of' link, not 'Same meaning'.
cast (the actors) = troupe (a group of performers); hex/shadow/spotlight/backdrop play on other senses of cast and are not groups.
vine = climber (a climbing plant), and the gloss pins the plant sense; the options are not climbers.
factory = mill (one WordNet synset: steel mill, paper mill); no option competes.
certify -> certification is the verb-to-noun form; the options have other roots.
minstrel = bard (travelling singer-poets, given as each other's synonyms); tango/duet/columnist do not compete.
hole = opening; peg fills a hole and a dent is a hollow, not an opening.
board = committee in the governing-group sense the gloss shows; the plank-sense traps are not groups.

Link (a): a festival is one kind of celebration, a special, organised, often religious or cultural one (Oxford: 'a day or period of celebration'). A birthday party or a win is a celebration but not a festival, so d is narrower than c, and 'Same meaning' teaches the 'A kind of' link under the wrong name. It also leaves 'graduation', another occasion that is celebrated, nearer than a clean distractor should be.
bard = minstrel; maiden/epic/ballad are not people of that kind.
circumference = girth (the distance around, as of a tree); the body-sense gloss is hidden and no option competes.
flip = somersault (MW: a somersault, especially in the air); upside/posit do not compete.
significance = meaning (the significance of a symbol); prestige is not, and meaningful/notable are adjectives.
bookshelf = bookcase in everyday use; alcove/workspace/attic are places.
blunt is the opposite of sharp; sour and strong are not opposites.
A baker is the one who bakes. Word families also fits but is not a better description.
A teacher is the one who teaches.
A sailor is the one who sails.
A painter is the one who paints.
A farmer is the one who farms.
A singer is the one who sings.
An actor is the one who acts.
A driver is the one who drives.
A swimmer is the one who swims.
An inventor is the one who invents.

Another link describes this pair better. 'cook' is just as commonly a NOUN, the person who cooks, so cook : chef reads most naturally as two people-words: Same meaning (thesauri give chef = cook), or a chef is a kind of cook (a professional one). As the A:B example it teaches 'synonym' and would steer a child to the synonym distractor (e.g. 'fragrance' in item:9p, perfume -> perfumer). Use a pair whose first word is only a verb.
A pilot is the person who flies the aircraft; pilot reads first as a person-noun.
A doctor is a person who heals (makes sick people well); common, kid-safe words.
A thief is a person who steals; story-common and kid-safe.
A tutor is a person who teaches. Minor: tutor is also a verb, but the person reading dominates.
A mechanic is a person who repairs machines.
A waiter is a person who serves food at tables.
A lifeguard is a person who rescues swimmers in danger (Cambridge: 'save them if they are in danger').
